balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Rollins, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Rollins, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Rollins, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Rollins, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Rollins, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Rollins, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Rollins, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Rollins, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by service line
segmentRevenue.content:
Rollins splits revenue into Residential pest control, Commercial pest control, Termite & ancillary services (termite treatment, crawlspace encapsulation, insulation, wildlife exclusion) and a small Franchise & other line.

For Rollins, Inc.: the mix is roughly 45% residential, 33% commercial, 22% termite & ancillary -- but the three lines are not growing together, so the mix shift matters as much as the total.

What to watch:

  • Residential's share shrinking as commercial and termite outgrow it
  • Acquisitions (26 in 2025, Romex in 2026) landing mostly in one segment

organicGrowth.title: Organic revenue growth by service line
organicGrowth.content:
Organic growth strips out acquisitions, isolating same-business volume and price gains for each service line.

For Rollins, Inc.: residential organic growth decelerated sharply through 2026 (to ~2.3% in Q3 2026) as AI/LLM search (ChatGPT, Gemini) disrupted the paid-search lead funnels residential marketing relied on; commercial (~6.6% in Q3 2026) and termite & ancillary held up far better, since they lean less on digital lead generation.

What to watch:

  • Whether residential stabilises as management reallocates marketing spend to AI search platforms
  • Commercial and termite continuing to outpace residential
  • Total organic growth versus reported revenue growth -- the gap is what M&A is adding

geoRevenue.title: US vs international revenue
geoRevenue.content:
Revenue split between the United States and international operations (Canada, UK, Australia and other markets, largely via owned operations and Orkin-branded franchises across ~71 countries).

For Rollins, Inc.: international is still only about 7% of revenue, so it is a growth option rather than a near-term driver of results -- the US pest control business is what moves the model.

What to watch:

  • Whether international grows faster than the US base (optionality) or just tracks it
  • Currency translation on the international line

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Rollins, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Rollins, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
